cards.title: The GCP Database Lineup at a Glance
cards.teaser: GCP offers six primary managed database services spanning relational, NoSQL document, wide-column, and in-memory tiers. Choosing the wrong one can mean paying 10x more or hitting hard scalability ceilings — a two-minute comparison table prevents both.

runs.text: Google Cloud manages databases across every major paradigm. The six core services and their positioning:

explanation.text:
Service       | Model            | Max Scale          | Consistency   | Best For
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cloud SQL     | Relational       | ~64 TB per DB      | Strong        | OLTP, lift-and-shift
AlloyDB       | Relational       | ~64 TB per DB      | Strong        | High-perf Postgres OLTP
Spanner       | NewSQL relational | Unlimited (sharded)| External      | Global OLTP, finance
Bigtable      | Wide-column NoSQL | Petabyte-scale     | Eventual*     | Time-series, IoT, ML
Firestore     | Document NoSQL   | ~1 million writes/s| Strong (doc)  | Mobile, real-time apps
Memorystore   | In-memory KV     | ~300 GB (Redis)    | Eventual      | Caching, session store

runs.text: Bigtable supports strong read-your-writes consistency within a cluster; cross-cluster replication is eventually consistent.

items.text: Cloud SQL and AlloyDB
both serve relational workloads but AlloyDB targets performance-critical Postgres use cases with a disaggregated storage engine.
Spanner
is the only service that combines full SQL, ACID transactions, and horizontal sharding at global scale.
Bigtable
is a low-latency column-family store — not a general-purpose database. It shines at high-throughput reads/writes with simple key lookups.
Firestore
is document-oriented with first-class mobile SDKs, offline support, and real-time listeners — the default choice for mobile/web frontends.
Memorystore
is a fully managed Redis, Memcached, or Valkey instance — no operations overhead for the most common caching patterns.

runs.text: GCP's six database services cover the entire spectrum: Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for standard relational work, Spanner for relational at global scale, Bigtable for massive-throughput key-value/time-series, Firestore for mobile document storage, and Memorystore for caching.

cards.title: Cloud SQL — Managed Relational for the Majority
cards.teaser: Cloud SQL is GCP's managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server service. It handles patches, backups, failover, and replication — eliminating the ops burden that keeps teams running self-managed databases on Compute Engine.

runs.text: Cloud SQL is the right default for any relational workload that fits within a single region and does not require multi-master writes at global scale. It supports MySQL 8.0, PostgreSQL 14/15/16, and SQL Server 2019/2022 — all running on the same managed infrastructure.
Key capabilities:

items.text: Automated maintenance windows
— minor version patches applied automatically during a user-specified window.
High availability
— a standby replica in a second zone in the same region with automatic failover; RPO near zero, RTO typically under 60 seconds.
Storage auto-increase
— disk grows automatically when usage nears the configured threshold (no manual resizing required).
Private IP via VPC peering or Private Service Access
— Cloud SQL instances connect to your VPC without traversing the public internet.
IAM database authentication
— users authenticate with IAM tokens instead of username/password, enabling centralized access control.

explanation.text:
# Create a Postgres 16 Cloud SQL instance
gcloud sql instances create my-pg-instance \
  --database-version=POSTGRES_16 \
  --tier=db-perf-optimized-N-4 \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --availability-type=REGIONAL \
  --storage-type=SSD \
  --storage-size=100GB

# Create a database
gcloud sql databases create mydb --instance=my-pg-instance

# Connect via Cloud SQL Auth Proxy (recommended over public IP)
gcloud sql auth-proxy my-pg-instance &

runs.text: Use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy for application connections. It handles IAM authentication and TLS encryption transparently, eliminating the need to allowlist application IPs or manage database user passwords.
Cloud SQL is managed MySQL/Postgres/SQL Server: Google handles patching, backups, and failover. You get a standard relational database without the ops overhead of running one yourself.

cards.title: AlloyDB — High-Performance Postgres on GCP
cards.teaser: AlloyDB is a Google-built Postgres-compatible database with a disaggregated, log-structured storage engine. It delivers ~4x faster transactional throughput than vanilla Cloud SQL Postgres and ~100x faster analytics queries — at the cost of higher base pricing.

runs.text: AlloyDB separates compute (primary + read pool instances) from storage (a distributed, multi-zone log store), enabling several capabilities that vanilla Postgres cannot achieve:

items.text: Read pool instances scale independently
— add or remove read replicas in seconds without any storage duplication, because all nodes share the same underlying storage.
Columnar engine for HTAP
— an optional in-memory columnar store transparently accelerates analytical queries on the same data used for transactions, without ETL.
Near-zero downtime maintenance
— compute nodes can be replaced without storage detachment, enabling maintenance windows that complete in under a minute.
Faster backups
— continuous WAL-based backups at the storage layer mean PITR does not require a full snapshot baseline.

runs.text: AlloyDB is wire-compatible with Postgres, so most Postgres drivers, ORMs, and tools work without modification.

explanation.text:
# Create an AlloyDB cluster
gcloud alloydb clusters create my-cluster \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --password=SUPER_SECRET

# Create a primary instance
gcloud alloydb instances create my-primary \
  --instance-type=PRIMARY \
  --cpu-count=4 \
  --cluster=my-cluster \
  --region=us-central1

# Add a read pool instance (3 nodes)
gcloud alloydb instances create my-read-pool \
  --instance-type=READ_POOL \
  --cpu-count=4 \
  --read-pool-node-count=3 \
  --cluster=my-cluster \
  --region=us-central1

runs.text: AlloyDB Omni is the self-managed, downloadable edition that runs in any environment (on-premises, other clouds). It provides the columnar engine and AlloyDB storage layer without GCP dependency — useful for hybrid scenarios.

AlloyDB is Google's reimplementation of Postgres with a faster storage engine. Same SQL, same drivers — but the underlying storage is Google-built and delivers roughly 4x more OLTP throughput than a standard Postgres instance.

cards.title: Spanner — NewSQL at Global Scale
cards.teaser: Cloud Spanner is the only database that combines full ANSI SQL, globally distributed horizontal sharding, and external consistency (stronger than serializability). It eliminates the traditional relational vs. scale trade-off — at the price of a fundamentally different schema design discipline.

runs.text: Spanner emerged from Google's 2012 OSDI paper. It was the internal system behind Google Ads, Gmail, and Google Play before being offered as a managed service. Its core claims:

items.text: Unlimited horizontal scale
— data is automatically split into tablets and distributed across nodes; adding nodes increases both storage and throughput linearly.
External consistency

— if transaction T2 starts after T1 commits (in real time), T2 will always observe T1's writes. This is stronger than serializability and enables correct distributed transactions without two-phase locking across regions.
Full SQL + ACID transactions
— not a subset SQL dialect; Spanner supports joins, subqueries, CTEs, window functions, and cross-row multi-table transactions.
99.999% SLA for multi-region configurations
— five nines means less than ~5 minutes of downtime per year.

runs.text: Spanner pricing is node-based (not storage-based), making small workloads expensive. A single-region instance starts at ~$0.90/node/hour. The sweet spot is high-scale OLTP where the equivalent sharded MySQL architecture would require significant engineering investment.

explanation.text:
# Create a Spanner instance (3 nodes, regional)
gcloud spanner instances create my-spanner \
  --config=regional-us-central1 \
  --description="Production OLTP" \
  --nodes=3

# Create a database
gcloud spanner databases create mydb --instance=my-spanner

# Query via gcloud
gcloud spanner databases execute-sql mydb \
  --instance=my-spanner \
  --sql="SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE status = 'pending' LIMIT 10"

runs.text: Spanner is not a drop-in replacement for MySQL or Postgres. It has its own DDL syntax, no auto-increment primary keys (use UUID or bit-reversal), and schema design constraints that differ from traditional RDBMS. Expect a migration investment.

Spanner is Google's "have both" database: it scales horizontally like a NoSQL system but gives you full SQL and ACID transactions. The catch is that it requires careful schema design and costs more than a standard relational database.

cards.title: Spanner TrueTime — How Global Consistency Works
cards.teaser: TrueTime is the atomic-clock-and-GPS timekeeping infrastructure that makes Spanner's external consistency possible. Understanding TrueTime explains why Spanner can commit globally consistent transactions without a centralized coordinator — and why commit-wait exists.

runs.text: Traditional distributed databases use logical clocks (Lamport clocks, vector clocks) to order events because physical clock skew between machines is unbounded and unpredictable. Spanner replaces logical clocks with TrueTime — a globally synchronized physical clock with a bounded uncertainty interval.
TrueTime architecture:

items.text: Each Google data center runs GPS-disciplined and atomic-clock-disciplined time masters.
Every server daemon polls multiple time masters and applies Marzullo's algorithm to compute a time interval
[earliest, latest]
that is guaranteed to contain the true absolute time.
The epsilon (uncertainty) is typically 1-7 ms — bounded, small, and publicly documented.

runs.text: Commit-wait protocol:

items.text: When a transaction is about to commit, Spanner assigns it a timestamp
s
drawn from the TrueTime interval's upper bound.
The coordinator then
waits
until TrueTime's earliest bound passes
s
— i.e., until the system is certain that no future transaction could receive a timestamp before
s

Only then does the commit return to the client. This "commit-wait" adds 1-10 ms latency per commit but guarantees that any subsequent transaction starting after this commit will receive a strictly higher timestamp — ensuring external consistency without any cross-region lock.

runs.text: TrueTime is the reason Spanner can do linearizable reads at a past timestamp across all nodes simultaneously. A "stale read" at timestamp T is guaranteed to be consistent — every node that has applied commits before T will return the same view of data.

TrueTime uses atomic clocks and GPS receivers in every data center to keep clocks tightly synchronized. Before a transaction finishes committing, Spanner waits until every clock in the system has definitely passed that transaction's timestamp — ensuring any later transaction observes the commit.

cards.title: Bigtable — Wide-Column NoSQL for Massive Throughput
cards.teaser: Cloud Bigtable is a fully managed HBase-compatible wide-column store designed for petabyte-scale workloads at sub-10 ms latency. Its model — rows with sparse column families — makes it ideal for time-series data, IoT streams, and ML feature stores, but wrong for relational or document workloads.

runs.text: Bigtable's data model is a sorted map: each row is identified by a single row key, and columns are organized into families. All reads and writes are by row key or row key range — there are no joins, no secondary indexes, and no query language beyond key range scans.

items.text: Row key
— the only index. Rows are sorted lexicographically by key. Key design drives performance entirely.
Column families
— groups of columns defined at schema creation time (e.g.,
stats
metadata
). Within a family, column qualifiers are arbitrary and can vary per row — the "wide" in wide-column.
Timestamps
— every cell stores multiple timestamped versions; garbage collection policies control retention.

runs.text: Bigtable scales by adding nodes to a cluster — throughput scales linearly (roughly 10,000 QPS per node for reads). Storage and compute are separated: storage lives in Colossus (Google's distributed filesystem), so adding/removing nodes does not require data movement.

explanation.text:
# Create a Bigtable instance
gcloud bigtable instances create my-bt \
  --display-name="My Bigtable" \
  --cluster=my-bt-cluster \
  --cluster-zone=us-central1-b \
  --cluster-num-nodes=3 \
  --cluster-storage-type=SSD

# Create a table and column family using cbt tool
cbt -instance=my-bt createtable metrics
cbt -instance=my-bt createfamily metrics stats

# Write and read a row
cbt -instance=my-bt set metrics "sensor#1234#20240101T120000" stats:temperature=22.5
cbt -instance=my-bt read metrics

runs.text: Bigtable has a minimum of 1 node per cluster. At less than ~300 GB of data, a single Bigtable instance is overkill — Firestore or Cloud SQL is almost always cheaper and simpler. Bigtable pays off at high volume (millions of rows/second) or very large datasets (hundreds of GB to petabytes).

Bigtable is a giant sorted key-value store where each value can have many columns organized into families. The entire access pattern is "look up by key" or "scan a range of keys" — no joins, no SQL. It's built for speed and volume, not flexibility.

cards.title: Firestore — Document NoSQL for Mobile and Web
cards.teaser: Firestore is a serverless, multi-region document database with real-time sync, offline support, and first-class mobile SDKs. It bills per operation rather than per node — making it cost-efficient at low to medium scale and the default choice for user-facing mobile and web applications.

runs.text: Firestore stores data as documents (JSON-like objects) organized into collections. Documents can contain subcollections, enabling hierarchical data models without foreign keys.

items.text: Real-time listeners
— clients subscribe to document or collection changes and receive updates via WebSocket-style push, enabling live-updating UIs without polling.
Offline support
— mobile SDKs (iOS, Android) cache data locally and sync changes when connectivity resumes; conflict resolution is handled by the SDK.
Transactions and batched writes
— atomic operations on up to 500 documents, with optimistic concurrency control.
Security rules
— Firebase Security Rules let you express access control logic directly in the database, enabling mobile apps to access Firestore without a backend server.
Automatic multi-region replication
— Firestore in Native mode replicates to multiple zones (regional) or multiple regions (multi-region) automatically.

explanation.text:
# Create a Firestore database (Native mode)
gcloud firestore databases create \
  --location=us-central \
  --type=firestore-native

# Export data to Cloud Storage
gcloud firestore export gs://my-backup-bucket/$(date +%F)

# Query via REST (example — most usage is via SDK)
curl -X POST \
  "https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/MY_PROJECT/databases/(default)/documents:runQuery" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"structuredQuery":{"from":[{"collectionId":"users"}],"limit":5}}'

runs.text: Firestore has two modes: Native mode (the current, recommended mode with real-time support) and Datastore mode (backward-compatible with the older Cloud Datastore API, without real-time listeners). Choose Native mode for all new projects.

Firestore is a document database that pushes updates to connected clients in real time. Think of it as a JSON store with a built-in pub/sub layer — perfect for mobile apps that need live data sync without managing websocket infrastructure.

cards.title: Memorystore — Managed In-Memory Caching
cards.teaser: Memorystore provides fully managed Redis, Memcached, and Valkey instances running inside your VPC. It offloads cache tier operations entirely — no cluster management, patching, or failover configuration — at the cost of vendor lock-in to GCP for your caching layer.

runs.text: Memorystore supports three engines:

items.text: Redis

— the most common choice. Supports rich data structures (lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes), Lua scripting, pub/sub, and Streams. Memorystore Redis Standard tier provides automatic failover with a read replica; Basic tier is single-node.
Memcached
— simple key-value caching. No persistence, no replication. Suitable for session caching where data loss is acceptable.
Valkey
— the open-source Redis fork (post-2024 license change). GCP added Valkey support to Memorystore; API-compatible with Redis 7.2.

runs.text: Common patterns:

items.text: Database query caching
— cache Cloud SQL or Spanner query results with a TTL; reduces database load for read-heavy workloads.
Session store
— stateless application servers store user sessions in Redis, enabling horizontal scaling of app tier.
Rate limiting
— Redis atomic increment + EXPIRE commands implement token bucket rate limiters without coordination across app instances.

explanation.text:
# Create a Redis Standard tier instance (with failover replica)
gcloud redis instances create my-cache \
  --size=5 \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --redis-version=redis_7_0 \
  --tier=STANDARD_HA

# Get connection details
gcloud redis instances describe my-cache --region=us-central1 \
  --format="value(host,port)"

# Create a Valkey instance
gcloud redis instances create my-valkey \
  --size=2 \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --engine=VALKEY \
  --engine-version=valkey_8_0

runs.text: Memorystore is managed Redis (or Memcached or Valkey) — you get a cache endpoint inside your VPC without running Redis yourself. Google handles patching and failover; you just connect your application.

cards.title: Cloud SQL Read Replicas — Scaling Reads Horizontally
cards.teaser: Cloud SQL read replicas offload read traffic from the primary instance and can be placed in different regions for latency-aware reads. They are asynchronous replicas — not HA standby nodes — which means replica lag must be factored into consistency requirements.

runs.text: A Cloud SQL read replica is an independent instance that replicates from the primary via MySQL binlog replication or Postgres streaming replication. Key characteristics:

items.text: Asynchronous replication
— writes committed on the primary reach the replica with a small lag (usually milliseconds, occasionally seconds under write bursts). Reading from a replica may return stale data.
Cross-region replicas
— a replica can be in a different region, enabling lower read latency for geographically distributed users.
Read replicas are not HA failover targets by default
— promotion to primary is a manual operation, not automatic. If automatic failover is needed, use the built-in HA standby (same-region, synchronous).
Cascading replicas
— a read replica can itself have downstream read replicas, reducing load on the primary for fan-out replication scenarios.

explanation.text:
# Create a read replica (same region)
gcloud sql instances create my-pg-replica \
  --master-instance-name=my-pg-instance \
  --region=us-central1

# Create a cross-region read replica
gcloud sql instances create my-pg-replica-eu \
  --master-instance-name=my-pg-instance \
  --region=europe-west1

# Monitor replica lag
gcloud sql instances describe my-pg-replica \
  --format="value(replicaConfiguration.failoverTarget,settings.databaseReplicationEnabled)"

runs.text: For Cloud SQL Postgres, you can promote a cross-region replica to become a new primary instance for disaster recovery. This is an irreversible operation — the replica detaches from the original primary and becomes a standalone instance.

Read replicas copy data from the primary and serve read traffic. They lag slightly behind the primary, so they are good for reports and read-heavy APIs but not for reads that must immediately reflect a recent write.

cards.title: Database Choice Flow — Picking the Right GCP Database
cards.teaser: The right GCP database depends on five orthogonal axes: data model, consistency requirements, scale, region distribution, and access pattern. A structured decision tree prevents the most common mistakes: choosing Spanner when Cloud SQL suffices, or using Firestore for analytics workloads.

runs.text: Decision tree (read top to bottom — stop at first match):

explanation.text:
START
  |
  v
Need an IN-MEMORY cache or message queue?
  YES --> Memorystore (Redis / Memcached / Valkey)
  NO
  |
  v
Primary access via DOCUMENTS with real-time sync or mobile SDK?
  YES --> Firestore (Native mode)
  NO
  |
  v
High-throughput KEY-VALUE / time-series (>10k ops/s, simple key lookups)?
  YES --> Bigtable
  NO
  |
  v
Need RELATIONAL schema + SQL + ACID transactions?
  NO  --> Re-evaluate (possibly Bigtable or Firestore)
  YES
  |
  v
Need GLOBAL distribution / multi-region strong consistency / >10 TB?
  YES --> Spanner
  NO
  |
  v
Need >4x Postgres throughput, HTAP (analytics on OLTP data),
or Postgres but with near-zero maintenance windows?
  YES --> AlloyDB
  NO
  |
  v
--> Cloud SQL (MySQL / Postgres / SQL Server)

runs.text: Secondary considerations:

items.text: If you have an existing MySQL/Postgres/SQL Server workload
and just want to stop managing infrastructure, Cloud SQL is the answer.
If your team is Postgres-native and you are CPU-bound on Cloud SQL
, evaluate AlloyDB before sharding or moving to Spanner.
If you need OLAP / data warehouse queries
(not OLTP), none of these six services is the right answer — use BigQuery.
Spanner's minimum cost is ~$0.90/node-hour
; never use it for small or cost-sensitive workloads below ~100 million rows.

runs.text: Start by asking what shape your data is. Cache? Memorystore. Documents with live sync? Firestore. Massive time-series key lookups? Bigtable. If you need SQL, then ask how big: global and huge goes to Spanner, high-performance Postgres goes to AlloyDB, everything else goes to Cloud SQL.

cards.title: Datastream — Change Data Capture as a Service
cards.teaser: Datastream is GCP's managed Change Data Capture (CDC) service. It reads the transaction logs of a source database and streams changes to a destination in near-real time — enabling event-driven architectures, data warehouse feeds, and zero-downtime database migrations.

runs.text: CDC means capturing every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE from a database's write-ahead log (WAL) or binlog as a stream of events — without polling the tables. Datastream operationalizes this as a fully managed service:

items.text: Sources
— Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, AlloyDB. Both on-premises and cloud-hosted.
Destinations
— BigQuery (direct table upserts), Cloud Storage (Avro/JSON/Parquet files), Cloud Spanner.
Backfill + ongoing CDC
— Datastream performs an initial full backfill of selected tables, then switches to log-based CDC. You get a complete, consistent copy from day 1.
Schema evolution
— Datastream detects DDL changes in the source and propagates compatible schema changes to the destination automatically.

explanation.text:
# Create a Datastream connection profile for a Postgres source
gcloud datastream connection-profiles create pg-source \
  --location=us-central1 \
  --type=postgresql \
  --postgresql-hostname=10.0.0.5 \
  --postgresql-port=5432 \
  --postgresql-username=datastream_user \
  --postgresql-password=SECRET \
  --postgresql-database=mydb

# Create a stream: Postgres -> BigQuery
gcloud datastream streams create pg-to-bq \
  --location=us-central1 \
  --display-name="Postgres to BigQuery" \
  --source=pg-source \
  --postgresql-source-config=source-config.json \
  --destination=bq-dest \
  --bigquery-destination-config=bq-config.json \
  --backfill-all

runs.text: Datastream to BigQuery is a common architecture for real-time analytics: OLTP data in Cloud SQL or AlloyDB feeds Datastream, which continuously upserts change events into BigQuery tables. Dashboards query BigQuery for analytics without touching the production database.

Datastream reads the change log of a source database and replays every insert, update, and delete to a destination in near-real time. It is the bridge between OLTP databases and analytical systems like BigQuery.

cards.title: Database Migration Service — Heterogeneous Migrations
cards.teaser: Database Migration Service (DMS) is GCP's managed tool for migrating databases to Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, or Spanner. It supports heterogeneous migrations (Oracle to Postgres, MySQL to Cloud SQL) with continuous replication, minimizing cutover downtime to seconds.

runs.text: DMS supports two migration modes:

items.text: Continuous migration

— performs a full dump of the source, restores it to the destination, then uses CDC (via Datastream under the hood) to keep destination in sync. Cutover is a planned switchover with seconds of downtime.
One-time migration
— single bulk export + import. Simpler but requires a maintenance window for cutover.

runs.text: Supported source-to-destination combinations:

items.text: MySQL → Cloud SQL for MySQL
PostgreSQL → Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL / AlloyDB
Oracle → Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL / AlloyDB (heterogeneous — requires schema conversion)
SQL Server → Cloud SQL for SQL Server

runs.text: Heterogeneous migrations (e.g., Oracle to Postgres) require schema and SQL conversion. DMS includes the
Database Migration Assessment
and
Schema Conversion Tool
(integrated with Gemini) to identify incompatible objects and suggest Postgres equivalents.

explanation.text:
# Create a DMS connection profile for source MySQL
gcloud database-migration connection-profiles create mysql-source \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --type=MYSQL \
  --host=10.0.0.10 \
  --port=3306 \
  --username=dms_user \
  --password=SECRET

# Create a migration job (continuous mode)
gcloud database-migration migration-jobs create mysql-to-cloudsql \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --type=CONTINUOUS \
  --source=mysql-source \
  --destination=cloudsql-dest

# Start the migration
gcloud database-migration migration-jobs start mysql-to-cloudsql \
  --region=us-central1

runs.text: DMS migrates your database to GCP with minimal downtime: it copies your data, then streams changes continuously so the destination stays in sync with the source. When you are ready to cut over, you pause writes to the source and flip your application to point at the destination.

cards.title: Backup and PITR — Cloud SQL Recovery Options
cards.teaser: Cloud SQL supports automated daily backups and point-in-time recovery (PITR) using write-ahead log archiving. PITR lets you restore a database to any second within the retention window — critical for recovery from accidental data deletion or corruption.

runs.text: Cloud SQL has two independent recovery mechanisms:

items.text: Automated backups
— daily snapshots of the entire database, retained for 1-365 days. Backups are stored in a Google-managed bucket in the instance's region. They enable restore to any backup snapshot.
Point-in-time recovery (PITR)

— Cloud SQL continuously archives transaction logs (binary logs for MySQL, WAL for Postgres) to Cloud Storage. Combined with a backup snapshot, PITR can restore the database to any second within the log retention window (1-35 days).

runs.text: PITR workflow:

items.text: 1. Restore the most recent backup snapshot before the target recovery time to a new instance.
2. Replay archived transaction logs from the backup point up to the target timestamp.
3. Verify data integrity, then redirect application connections.

explanation.text:
# Enable PITR and configure backup settings
gcloud sql instances patch my-pg-instance \
  --backup-start-time=02:00 \
  --enable-point-in-time-recovery \
  --retained-backups-count=14 \
  --retained-transaction-log-days=7

# List available backups
gcloud sql backups list --instance=my-pg-instance

# Restore to a specific point in time (creates a new instance)
gcloud sql instances restore-backup my-pg-instance \
  --restore-instance=my-pg-restored \
  --backup-id=BACKUP_ID

# PITR: restore to a specific timestamp
gcloud sql instances clone my-pg-instance my-pg-pitr \
  --point-in-time=2024-06-15T14:30:00.000Z

runs.text: PITR restores to a new instance — it does not overwrite the existing instance. You must redirect application connections manually after verifying the restored instance. Plan the cutover procedure before you need to execute it under pressure.

Backups are daily snapshots; PITR uses those snapshots plus a continuous stream of transaction logs to recover to any moment in time. If someone accidentally deletes a table at 2:47 PM, PITR lets you restore the database to 2:46 PM.

cards.title: Bigtable Replication — Multi-Region Active-Active
cards.teaser: Bigtable supports multi-cluster replication across regions, with all clusters accepting both reads and writes simultaneously. This active-active topology enables low-latency reads near users, zero-RPO disaster recovery, and read-write isolation — but requires designing around eventual consistency.

runs.text: Bigtable replication is asynchronous and eventually consistent across clusters. A write to Cluster A in us-central1 will replicate to Cluster B in europe-west1 with a lag typically in the range of tens of milliseconds to a few seconds.
Key replication topologies:

items.text: Multi-region active-active

— two or more clusters in different regions, all accepting reads and writes. Applications route to the nearest cluster. Conflicts (concurrent writes to the same row) are resolved by last-write-wins at cell level.
Read-write isolation
— one cluster accepts all writes; a second cluster serves reads only. Useful for isolating analytics queries from OLTP traffic.
Single-cluster zone failover
— a second cluster in the same region but different zone provides HA within a region with synchronous availability (Bigtable uses 3-zone redundancy within a regional cluster).

explanation.text:
# Add a replication cluster to an existing Bigtable instance
gcloud bigtable clusters create my-bt-cluster-eu \
  --instance=my-bt \
  --zone=europe-west1-b \
  --num-nodes=3 \
  --storage-type=SSD

# Configure an app profile for multi-cluster routing
gcloud bigtable app-profiles update default \
  --instance=my-bt \
  --route-any \
  --transactional-writes

# App profile for read-write isolation (writes to primary cluster only)
gcloud bigtable app-profiles create write-only \
  --instance=my-bt \
  --route-to-cluster=my-bt-cluster \
  --transactional-writes

runs.text: App profiles are Bigtable's mechanism for routing requests to specific clusters or for multi-cluster round-robin. Each client configuration specifies an app profile ID, enabling different routing policies for different workloads within the same instance.

Bigtable can replicate your data to clusters in multiple regions, with every cluster accepting writes simultaneously. Changes flow between clusters asynchronously — there is no global lock — so you get low-latency local writes everywhere, at the cost of eventual consistency.

cards.title: Spanner Schema Design — Interleaved Tables and Hot Spots
cards.teaser: Spanner's performance depends critically on primary key choice and interleaved table design. A poor primary key causes write hot spots that limit throughput to a single split — regardless of how many nodes you have. Understanding interleaving and key distribution is the first Spanner design skill.

runs.text: Spanner distributes data across splits (key ranges stored on separate servers). Throughput scales when writes are distributed across splits — and degrades when they concentrate on one.
Primary key anti-patterns that create hot spots:

items.text: Auto-incrementing integers
— all new writes go to the highest key range (the "end" of the table). One split handles all inserts. Use UUID v4 or bit-reversed sequences instead.
Monotonically increasing timestamps as leading key
— same problem as auto-increment. Prefix with a hash or shard ID.
Low-cardinality leading key
— e.g., a boolean or small enum as the first primary key column concentrates traffic on two to five splits.

runs.text: Interleaved tables:

items.text: Interleaving co-locates child rows with their parent row on the same split.
This eliminates cross-split joins for parent-child lookups — the most common Spanner performance optimization.
The child table's primary key must start with the parent table's primary key columns.

explanation.text:
-- Parent table with UUID primary key (no hot spots)
CREATE TABLE Orders (
  OrderId   STRING(36) NOT NULL,  -- UUID
  CustomerId STRING(36) NOT NULL,
  Status    STRING(20),
  CreatedAt TIMESTAMP,
) PRIMARY KEY (OrderId);

-- Child table interleaved with Orders
-- OrderItems rows are stored adjacent to their parent Order row
CREATE TABLE OrderItems (
  OrderId    STRING(36) NOT NULL,  -- same leading key as parent
  ItemId     STRING(36) NOT NULL,
  ProductId  STRING(36),
  Quantity   INT64,
) PRIMARY KEY (OrderId, ItemId),
  INTERLEAVE IN PARENT Orders ON DELETE CASCADE;

runs.text: Use INTERLEAVE IN PARENT whenever you have a one-to-many relationship where you frequently read a parent with its children (e.g., fetch Order with all its OrderItems). It turns a distributed join into a local scan, which is orders of magnitude faster at Spanner scale.

In Spanner, data is split by key range across servers. If all your inserts go to the same end of the key range (like auto-increment IDs), all writes hit one server. Use random IDs (UUIDs) to spread inserts across splits. Interleaving stores child records physically next to their parent, making parent-child reads fast.
